extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, investigators, decisionmakers, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and implementation guidance for §106.46 grievance procedures at postsecondary institutions, including rules on advisors, support persons, expert witnesses, timeframes, and access to evidence under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to an advisor of choice
rubrics_metrics.description: A party has a right to select an advisor of choice, and that advisor may be an attorney; the advisor is not required to be an attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with §106.45(b)(5)(iv) of the 2020 amendments, §106.46(e)(2) permits an attorney as advisor. The status of an advisor and financial resources of a party must not affect an institution's compliance with §§106.45 and 106.46. Institutions are not required to pay for parties' advisors, but may choose to provide or pay for advisors; parties retain the right to select and decline institution-offered advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor presence in meetings and proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must not limit the presence of a party's advisor in any meeting or proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While institutions may establish restrictions on the extent of advisor participation, they may not prevent an advisor from being present for meetings or proceedings. Any restrictions on advisor participation must apply equally to both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on advisor participation (scope and equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions may restrict the extent to which an advisor may participate in proceedings, provided restrictions are applied equally to both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to remove institutional discretion to limit advisor participation to preserve orderly and efficient proceedings. If an institution permits questioning by an advisor at a live hearing under §106.46(f)(1)(ii)(B), it must allow the party's advisor of choice to conduct the questioning. The regulations do not specify permissible restriction types; institutions judge appropriate functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution-appointed advisors for live-hearing questioning (confidential employee prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an institution is required to appoint an advisor to ask questions on behalf of a party during advisor-conducted questioning at a live hearing, the institution may not appoint a confidential employee to serve as that advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.46(f)(1)(ii)(B) was revised to prohibit appointment of confidential employees as institution-appointed advisors for questioning because doing so may jeopardize the employee's ability to serve as a confidential employee and risk protected communications. A party may nevertheless choose a confidential employee as their own advisor of choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential employees as voluntary advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may choose a confidential employee to serve as their advisor of choice, but the institution may not require or appoint a confidential employee as the institution's advisor when appointment is compelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although concerns exist about confidentiality and disclosure under §106.45(b)(7)(i), preserving party choice permits a party to select a confidential employee despite those concerns. Institutions should advise parties of potential complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor who is also a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may select an advisor who has served or may serve as a witness; institutions should not prohibit such selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with prior Department positions, prohibiting an advisor-witness is inappropriate. Decisionmakers may consider conflicts of interest and whether the advisor-witness was exposed to information in their advisor role that could influence testimony when weighing credibility. Institutions may advise parties of potential complications of choosing an advisor who may be called as a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mandatory advisor training requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions are not required to mandate training for advisors, though they may offer training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to require recipients to mandate advisor training because such a requirement could limit parties' ability to select advisors based on whether they have received training. Nothing prohibits recipients from providing advisor training voluntarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodating advisor availability and time extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must allow reasonable extensions of timeframes on a case-by-case basis for good cause (e.g., to accommodate advisor availability), while remaining mindful of reasonably prompt timeframes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under §106.46(e)(5), recipients must allow reasonable timeline extensions for good cause but must also meet their own obligations to conduct proceedings in a reasonably prompt manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of persons other than advisors (support persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions may permit parties to have persons other than their advisor present as support at meetings or proceedings, at the institution's discretion, provided equal opportunities are afforded to the parties and other legal obligations are observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.46(e)(3) gives institutions discretion to allow additional persons (e.g., support persons, parents, union representatives) but that discretion is constrained by FERPA and other laws. If allowing such persons would violate FERPA, the institution may not permit them unless prior written consent or a constitutional override applies. ADA/Section 504 and Title VI may require provision of support persons (interpreters, auxiliary aids) to ensure effective communication and equal opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parents and postsecondary students
rubrics_metrics.description: A parent or guardian is not automatically entitled to attend proceedings for a postsecondary student; institutions have discretion to permit parents but must not allow presence that would violate FERPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.6(g) does not create an automatic right for parents of postsecondary students to attend; postsecondary students are typically more independent. A recipient must not permit a parent/guardian to attend if their presence would violate FERPA. Parties may choose a parent as their advisor if they wish.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mandatory limits on number of support persons or confidentiality agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions are not required to limit the number of persons who may accompany a party or require attendees to sign confidentiality agreements; institutions should balance privacy concerns and FERPA obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.46(e)(3) must be interpreted consistent with FERPA; reasonable steps to protect privacy (including confidentiality agreements where appropriate) are permitted but not mandated. Clery Act requirements may separately apply in certain sexual violence-related proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion to allow expert witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions have discretion to decide whether to allow expert witnesses; they are not required to permit experts in all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department neither encourages nor discourages expert witnesses. Because experts did not observe the alleged conduct, their testimony may be unnecessary and may prolong proceedings. Institutions should weigh facts and circumstances to balance promptness, fairness, and accuracy. Parties may explain why expert testimony would be helpful. Institutions must exercise discretion in a manner consistent with obligations to objectively evaluate relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence, treat parties equitably, and use unbiased investigators/decisionmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character witnesses and relevance requirement for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Character witnesses and other character evidence are permitted only if the evidence is relevant and not otherwise impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(f)(2) permits relevant and not otherwise impermissible character evidence. Whether a character witness is relevant depends on the facts and circumstances and must aid the decisionmaker in determining whether sex-based harassment occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence (evidence vs investigative report option)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must provide parties and their advisors an equal opportunity to access the relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence either by (a) providing access to the underlying evidence or (b) providing a written investigative report that accurately summarizes the evidence; if the institution initially provides only an investigative report and a party requests the underlying evidence, the institution must provide access to the underlying evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.46(e)(6)(i) requires an equal opportunity to access relevant evidence. Institutions need not provide physical or electronic copies but must allow access. The change from 'directly related' to 'relevant' (defined in §106.2) limits scope; parties may not access evidence regarding a complainant's sexual predisposition or prior sexual behavior except in two narrow exceptions (§106.45(b)(7)(iii)). A decisionmaker cannot rely on evidence that the parties were not given access to, and the written determination must include the decisionmaker's evaluation of the relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance standard and limits on access to certain sexual-history evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations adopt a 'relevant' standard (defined in §106.2) for evidence access and exclude broad access to evidence regarding a complainant's sexual predisposition or prior sexual conduct except where narrowly permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department replaced the 'directly related' standard with 'relevant' to align scope with what aids a decisionmaker. Evidence about a complainant's sexual interests or prior sexual conduct is not accessible unless it (1) is offered to prove someone other than the respondent committed the conduct or (2) concerns specific incidents of the complainant's prior sexual conduct with the respondent and is offered to prove consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a party's nonappearance at a live hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party chooses not to attend a live hearing, their advisor retains the right to ask relevant and not otherwise impermissible questions, but the decisionmaker may place less or no weight on statements made by the nonappearing party; the decisionmaker must not draw an inference solely based on a party's refusal to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under §106.46(f)(1)(ii)(B) and §106.46(f)(4), a party may have their advisor ask questions even if the party does not appear; however, nonappearance may justify less weight on that party's statements. The decisionmaker cannot infer whether sex-based harassment occurred based solely on refusal to respond.
